summary: Defines how IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies are carried over FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network. It is a standards-track document describing the encapsulation used on those networks.

plainLanguage.summary: FDDI is a fibre ring network, and its link layer is not the same as Ethernet's. This document says how to carry IP traffic and address lookups on it: the extra headers that go in front of every packet, how a hardware address is found for a given IP address, how multicast addresses are chosen, and how large a packet may be. It also lists the little control values the 802.2 LLC layer uses, in the two bit orders the two worlds write numbers in.

questions: how is ip sent over fddi
how does arp work on fddi
how is ip carried over fddi
subtitle: How IP datagrams and ARP are carried on FDDI fibre rings, and the bit orders the two worlds use.

tldr.problem: FDDI is a token ring network whose link layer does not look like Ethernet, so IP and ARP needed an agreed way to be carried on it, including the address mapping and the bit order of MAC addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The document specifies 802.2 LLC and SNAP encapsulation: a DSAP and SSAP of 170, a control value of 3 for Unnumbered Information, and a SNAP header whose organization code is zero so that the EtherType can follow. ARP runs with the Ethernet hardware type code so that bridges can pass the packets.
tldr.outcome: IP multicast addresses map into the FDDI group address 01-00-5E-00-00-00, the MTU of an FDDI network is fixed at 4352 octets, and the document lists the LLC control values and the IEEE and Internet bit orders for each of them.

today: RFC 1188 is a Draft Standard published in October 1990 and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 1103 and describes the encapsulation of IP and ARP on FDDI networks: the 802.2 LLC and SNAP headers, the ARP fields and their bit order, the multicast mapping and the size limits.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The goal of this specification is to allow compatible and interoperable implementations for transmitting IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies.

The Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) family of standards provides the Physical Layer and the Media Access Control sublayer of the Data Link Layer as defined in the ISO Open Systems Interconnection reference model. The rest of the Data Link Service comes from the IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control service, so the stack looks like this: IP and ARP on top, then 802.2 LLC, then the FDDI MAC, PHY and PMD layers.

The document describes the use of IP and ARP in that environment. It notes that the use of IP and ARP does not yet have to be consistent between FDDI and IEEE 802 networks, but the intent is not to preclude Data Link Layer interoperability when the standards define it. FDDI defines both single and dual MAC stations, and the document covers single MAC stations only, whether single-attach or dual-attach; operation on dual MAC stations is left to a forthcoming document.
sections.plainLanguage: FDDI is a fibre ring network with its own link layer, and this document says how IP and the address lookup protocol ride on it. It covers stations with one network interface, either single-attached or dual-attached, and leaves the dual-interface case to a later document.

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies sent on FDDI networks are encapsulated within the 802.2 LLC and Sub-Network Access Protocol data link layers and the FDDI MAC and physical layers. The SNAP header must be used with an Organization Code that says the header holds the EtherType code.

802.2 LLC Type 1 communication, which every conforming 802.2 station must implement, is used exclusively. All frames are transmitted in the standard 802.2 LLC Type 1 Unnumbered Information format, with the DSAP and the SSAP fields of the 802.2 header set to the assigned global SAP value for SNAP, which is 170. The 24-bit Organization Code in the SNAP is zero, and the remaining 16 bits are the EtherType from Assigned Numbers: 2048 for IP and 2054 for ARP. The total length of the LLC header and the SNAP header is 8 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IP or ARP packet on FDDI carries 8 octets of extra header. The first three octets say which service the packet belongs to, using the number 170, and that the frame is an unnumbered information frame. The next three octets are zero, and the last two carry the EtherType, which is 2048 for IP and 2054 for ARP.

sections.title: Address Resolution
sections.content:
The mapping of 32-bit Internet addresses to 48-bit FDDI addresses is done with the dynamic discovery procedure of the Address Resolution Protocol. Internet addresses are assigned arbitrarily on Internet networks, so each host's implementation must know its own Internet address and respond to address resolution requests appropriately, and it must use ARP to translate Internet addresses to FDDI addresses when needed.

ARP has several fields that parameterise its use: the hardware type code and the protocol type code, both 16 bits, the number of octets in each hardware address and in each protocol address, both 8 bits, and the 16-bit operation code. The hardware type code assigned for IEEE 802 networks is 6 and the one for Ethernet networks is 1. The differing values cause interoperability problems in bridged environments, so ARP packets are transmitted with a hardware type code of 1, and are accepted if received with either 1 or 6. The protocol type code for IP is 2048, the hardware address length is 6, the protocol address length for IP is 4, and the operation code is 1 for a request and 2 for a reply.

The hardware addresses in ARP packets, the sender and target hardware addresses, must be carried in canonical bit order, with the Group bit as the low order bit of the first octet. FDDI addresses are normally written with the Group bit in the high order bit position, so the addresses must be bit-reversed within each octet. The document also recommends that MAC addresses be represented in canonical order in all network layer protocols carried in the information field of an FDDI frame.
sections.plainLanguage: A host that wants to send to an IP address asks the network which hardware address goes with it, using ARP. The reply carries the 48-bit FDDI address, written in the bit order that Ethernet uses rather than the one FDDI normally uses, so that a bridge between the two can pass the packet along. The reply is accepted whether it claims to be Ethernet or IEEE 802.

sections.title: Broadcast and Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
The broadcast Internet address, the address on that network with a host part of all binary ones, must be mapped to the broadcast FDDI address, which is also of all binary ones.

A method of supporting IP multicasting is specified in a separate document, and that method must be used on FDDI networks if IP multicasting is to be supported. Its use may require the ability to copy frames addressed to any one of an arbitrary number of multicast group addresses. An IP multicast address is mapped to an FDDI group address by placing the low order 23 bits of the IP address into the low order 23 bits of the FDDI group address 01-00-5E-00-00-00, in canonical order. The document gives the worked example: the IP multicast address 224.255.0.2 maps to the FDDI group address 01-00-5E-7F-00-02, in which the multicast group bit is the low order bit of the first octet. Bit-reversed for transmission in the destination MAC address field of an FDDI frame, in native order, that address becomes 80-00-7A-FE-00-40, with the multicast group bit as the high order bit of the first octet, that being the first bit transmitted on the medium.
sections.plainLanguage: Broadcast is simple: the all-ones address on IP becomes the all-ones address on FDDI. Multicast needs a fixed prefix: the last 23 bits of the IP group address are copied into a reserved FDDI group address that starts 01-00-5E, and the result is then bit-reversed for transmission, which is why the same group address is written two ways in the document.

sections.title: Packet Size and the MTU
sections.content:
The FDDI MAC specification defines a maximum frame size of 9000 symbols, 4500 octets, for all frame fields, including four symbols, two octets, of preamble. That leaves roughly 4470 octets for data once the LLC and SNAP header is taken into account. Because it is desirable to reserve additional space for MAC overhead and possible future extensions to the MAC header and frame status fields, the MTU of FDDI networks is 4352 octets, which provides 4096 octets of data and 256 octets of headers at the network layer and above. Implementations must not send packets larger than the MTU.

Gateway implementations must be prepared to accept packets as large as the MTU and to fragment them when necessary, and should be able to accept packets as large as can be carried within a maximum size FDDI frame and fragment them. Host implementations should be prepared to accept packets as large as the MTU, but hosts must not send datagrams longer than 576 octets unless they have explicit knowledge that the destination is prepared to accept them; a host may communicate its size preference in TCP-based applications through the TCP Maximum Segment Size option. Datagrams on FDDI networks may be longer than the general Internet default maximum packet size of 576 octets, so a host sending to a host that is not on the same local network should keep that in mind, and it may be appropriate to send smaller datagrams to avoid unnecessary fragmentation at intermediate gateways.

There is no minimum packet size restriction on FDDI networks. In order not to preclude interoperability with Ethernet in a bridged environment, FDDI implementations must be prepared to receive, and ignore, trailing pad octets.
sections.plainLanguage: A frame on FDDI can be much larger than an Ethernet frame, but the document fixes the usable packet size at 4352 octets, leaving room for headers. Hosts should not send more than 576 octets unless they know the receiver can take it, and gateways split up anything larger. There is no minimum size, and padding at the end of a frame is to be ignored.

sections.title: MAC and LLC Operation
sections.content:
FDDI defines two classes of LLC frames, asynchronous and synchronous. Asynchronous frames are further controlled by a priority mechanism and two classes of token, restricted and unrestricted. Only the use of unrestricted tokens and asynchronous frames is required for FDDI interoperability, so all IP and ARP frames are transmitted as asynchronous LLC frames using unrestricted tokens, and the priority value is a matter of local convention. It is recommended that implementations also accept IP and ARP packets in synchronous frames and in restricted asynchronous frames.

After transmission, FDDI provides Frame Copied and Address Recognized indicators, and their use is a local implementation decision: an implementation may use them to perform link-level retransmission or to invalidate ARP cache entries. The semantics of these indicators, especially in the presence of bridges, are not well defined as of this writing.

The FDDI MAC specification does not require that 16-bit and 48-bit address stations interwork fully, but it does require that 16-bit stations have full 48-bit functionality and that both types can receive frames sent to either size of broadcast address. To avoid interoperability problems, only 48-bit addresses are used with IP and ARP.

On the 802.2 side, all implementations must support the IEEE 802.2 standard Class I service in order to be compliant with 802.2. Class I LLC requires support for Unnumbered Information commands, eXchange IDentification commands and responses, and TEST link commands and responses; stations need not be able to transmit XID and TEST commands, but must be able to transmit responses. Command frames are identified by having the low order bit of the SSAP address reset to zero, and response frames by that bit set to one. The UI command has an LLC control field value of 3; the XID command and response have a control value of 175, or 191 with the Poll/Final bit on; the TEST command and response have a control value of 227, or 243 with the Poll/Final bit on.

As for the elements of procedure, UI responses and UI commands with the Poll bit set are ignored, and UI commands with anything other than the SNAP SAP in the DSAP or SSAP fields are not processed as IP or ARP packets. An XID or TEST command must be answered, but only when the DSAP is the SNAP SAP, 170, the Null SAP, 0, or the Global SAP, 255, unless the station supports the addressed service. The response copies the source MAC address of the command into the destination MAC field, sets the source MAC to its own address, copies the SSAP of the command into the DSAP, and sets the SSAP to 171 when the command used the SNAP or Global SAP, or to 1 when it used the Null SAP. The Final bit in the response is copied from the Poll bit in the command, XID responses include an 802.2 XID information field of 129.1.0 indicating Class I service, and TEST responses echo the information field they received.
sections.plainLanguage: IP and ARP frames are sent as ordinary asynchronous frames with the unrestricted token, so that every FDDI station can read them. On the 802.2 side, the station must answer the identification and test commands that other stations use to check whether anyone is present, and it must ignore anything that is not addressed to the service it implements.

sections.title: Byte Order and Number Conversions
sections.content: As described in the Internet Protocol specification, the IP datagram is transmitted over FDDI networks as a series of 8-bit bytes, an order that has been called big-endian. The IEEE, however, specifies numbers as bit strings with the least significant bit first, in a bit-wise little-endian order, and the Internet protocols are documented in a bit-wise big-endian order. That difference causes confusion about the values to use for numbers, so the document ends with a table of conversions for the numbers that matter: the UI control value, the SAP for SNAP, the Global SAP, the Null SAP, the XID and XID Poll/Final values, the XID information field 129.1.0, and the TEST and TEST Poll/Final values, each in IEEE binary, Internet binary and Internet decimal.
sections.plainLanguage: The two standards write the same number down differently: the IEEE writes it least significant bit first, the Internet protocols most significant bit first. The document's last table gives both forms, plus the decimal value, for every number used in the protocol, so an implementer does not have to work it out.
